domain_restrictions: f is a total function from the Euclidean plane R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}

the hypothesis applies only to triples A,B,C that are noncollinear (hence distinct) so the circumcenter is uniquely defined in R^2
the circumcenter operation circ(A,B,C) is the unique intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (uses Euclidean geometry)
root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c. Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].

assume (hypothesis) forall A,B,C in R^2: if A,B,C are noncollinear and f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A)
conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Start with the given circumcenter-closure hypothesis for monochromatic noncollinear triples. First convert it into a circle formulation: any three distinct same-colored points on a circle force the center of that circle to have that color (A1 via L1). From this, deduce that each circle centered at P has at most two points of color different from P (A2 via L2). Next analyze a bichromatic segment AB: the two equilateral completion points on AB must split the two colors, one matching A and one matching B (A3 via L3). This creates a purely discrete local rule on every affine copy of the triangular lattice. The coloring-specific lattice rigidity lemma L4 then implies that every affine triangular lattice is monochromatic; L5 transfers and packages this fact for arbitrary translated/scaled lattices in the plane (A4). Finally, any two plane points lie in a common affine triangular lattice, so if every such lattice is monochromatic, the whole plane is monochromatic; this is exactly L6, giving the root conclusion (A5).

steps.derives: From the root hypothesis on f, derive that whenever P is a point, r>0, and X,Y,Z are three distinct points on S(P,r) of one common color, then P has that same color.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 directly to the given coloring f. The root hypothesis is exactly the premise required by L1.

steps.derives: For every point P and every radius r>0, the circle S(P,r) contains at most two points whose color differs from f(P).
steps.trivial_justification: L2 applies to the centered-circle implication obtained in A1. Therefore every centered circle is almost monochromatic in the color of its center.

steps.derives: For any two points A,B with different colors, the two equilateral completion points on segment AB split the two colors: one matches A and one matches B.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of L3 from the circle-exception property established in A2.

steps.derives: Every affine copy T_{O,s} of the triangular lattice is monochromatic under f.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix arbitrary O and s>0. By A3, the restriction of f to T_{O,s} satisfies the bichromatic-edge equilateral-completion rule required for L4, because every unit-edge statement in L4 transfers by similarity to an edge of length s in T_{O,s}. Therefore L4 shows the restriction is constant. Since O and s were arbitrary, L5 packages this conclusion as: every affine triangular lattice T_{O,s} is monochromatic.

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red, green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L6 to the statement proved in A4 that every affine triangular lattice is monochromatic. L6 yields exactly that the entire plane has one color.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red, green} be a coloring with the following property: whenever A,B,C are noncollinear points of the plane and f(A)=f(B)=f(C), one has f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A). Let P be any point of the plane, let r>0, and let X,Y,Z be three distinct points on the circle S(P,r). If f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z), then f(P)=f(X).

lemmas.role_in_assembly: This is the key local consequence: every circle centered at P is almost monochromatic in the color of P.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red, green} be a coloring with the following property: for every point P of the plane, every real number r>0, and every three distinct points X,Y,Z on the circle S(P,r), if f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z) then f(P)=f(X). Fix any point P in R^2 and any radius r>0. Then the circle S(P,r) contains at most two points whose color is different from f(P). Equivalently, every point of S(P,r) except possibly two has color f(P).

lemmas.self_check_notes: On S(A,AB), the points B,U,V lie; since B has color opposite to A, at most one of U,V can also be opposite to A, so at least one matches A. Similarly on S(B,AB), at least one of U,V matches B. Because there are only two colors and only two points U,V, the conclusion follows.

lemmas.statement_nl: Consider the standard unit triangular lattice T = {m(1,0) + n(1/2, sqrt(3)/2) : m,n in Z} in the Euclidean plane. Let g : T -> {red, green} be a coloring of the lattice vertices such that for every pair of lattice points A,B with AB = 1 and g(A) != g(B), if U and V are the two lattice points for which triangles AUB and AVB are equilateral of side length 1, then among U and V exactly one has color g(A) and exactly one has color g(B). Under these assumptions, g is constant on T.

candidates.strategy_summary: Unlike the failed attempts, this strategy does not classify arbitrary circumcenter-closed subsets of the plane (which was false, as shown by the Q^2 counterexample). Instead it keeps the full 2-coloring context and first converts the circumcenter hypothesis into a circle-based 'at most two exceptions on every centered circle' property, then uses a coloring-specific structural lemma about such circle-exception colorings to conclude constancy.
